questions.prompt: Limiting photosynthesisAt a fixed temperature, a plant absorbs 2.4 mg of carbon dioxide in 4 minutes at light setting A and 4.8 mg in 4 minutes at setting B. Doubling the light again gives no further increase. A grower proposes heating the greenhouse all night to increase photosynthesis. Evaluate this proposal.
scheme: 1 · No photosynthesis without light at night (1).
2 · Heating costs money/energy and may not raise yield enough to cover costs (1).
3 · It may be useful only with lighting and sufficient carbon dioxide, or for preventing cold damage; conclusion must link to conditions (1).

questions.prompt: Metabolism and exerciseA person runs at increasing speed until oxygen delivery can no longer meet demand. Explain the relationship between respiration and metabolism.
scheme: 1 · Respiration transfers energy from glucose (1).
2 · This energy supports metabolic reactions such as protein synthesis or conversion of glucose to glycogen (1).

questions.prompt: Metabolism and exerciseA person runs at increasing speed until oxygen delivery can no longer meet demand. Explain why anaerobic respiration leads to muscle fatigue and an oxygen debt.
scheme: 1 · Glucose is incompletely broken down to lactic acid (1).
2 · Lactic acid accumulation contributes to fatigue (1).
3 · Extra oxygen is required after exercise to react with/remove the lactic acid (1).

questions.prompt: Metabolism and exerciseA person runs at increasing speed until oxygen delivery can no longer meet demand. Describe how lactic acid is processed after exercise.
scheme: 1 · Transported in blood from muscles to liver (1).
2 · Converted back into glucose in the liver (1).
3 · Oxygen/energy is required during recovery; accept some glucose stored as glycogen (1).

questions.prompt: Metabolism and exerciseA person runs at increasing speed until oxygen delivery can no longer meet demand. Compare anaerobic respiration in yeast with that in muscles.
scheme: 1 · Yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; muscles produce lactic acid (1).
2 · Both transfer energy without oxygen/from incomplete breakdown of glucose (1).

questions.prompt: Assessing an antiseptic claimAn antiseptic company compares equal discs on agar seeded with one approved bacterial strain. Mean inhibition diameters are control: 6 mm; low concentration: 10 mm; high concentration: 14 mm. All discs are 6 mm wide. The company claims its product kills every type of pathogen. Calculate the clear-zone area outside the high-concentration disc, using π = 3.14.
scheme: 1 · Outer radius = 7 mm and disc radius = 3 mm.
2 · Subtract areas: π(7² − 3²).
3 · Area = 125.6 mm².

questions.prompt: Assessing an antiseptic claimAn antiseptic company compares equal discs on agar seeded with one approved bacterial strain. Mean inhibition diameters are control: 6 mm; low concentration: 10 mm; high concentration: 14 mm. All discs are 6 mm wide. The company claims its product kills every type of pathogen. Explain why the claim is not justified.
scheme: 1 · Only one bacterial strain was tested, not every pathogen.
2 · Inhibition of visible growth does not prove all cells were killed.
3 · The claim extends beyond the experimental conditions / ignores viruses, fungi or other untested pathogens.

questions.prompt: Assessing an antiseptic claimAn antiseptic company compares equal discs on agar seeded with one approved bacterial strain. Mean inhibition diameters are control: 6 mm; low concentration: 10 mm; high concentration: 14 mm. All discs are 6 mm wide. The company claims its product kills every type of pathogen. Describe two precautions that reduce contamination and one school incubation precaution.
scheme: 1 · Sterilise medium / equipment.
2 · Open lids briefly and use aseptic inoculation.
3 · Incubate at 25°C and do not reopen incubated plates.

questions.prompt: Assessing an antiseptic claimAn antiseptic company compares equal discs on agar seeded with one approved bacterial strain. Mean inhibition diameters are control: 6 mm; low concentration: 10 mm; high concentration: 14 mm. All discs are 6 mm wide. The company claims its product kills every type of pathogen. Why report several independent plates rather than a single plate?
scheme: 1 · To assess variation and improve reliability of a mean.

questions.prompt: Targeted antibody deliveryA tumour has antigen X on many of its cells. Scientists make a monoclonal antibody against X and attach a drug. In a trial, 42 of 70 treated patients improve, compared with 21 of 70 receiving the comparison treatment. Describe how a hybridoma producing the antibody is made.
scheme: 1 · Expose a mouse to the antigen and obtain antibody-producing lymphocytes.
2 · Fuse lymphocytes with tumour cells.
3 · Select and clone a suitable hybridoma to produce identical antibodies.

questions.prompt: Targeted antibody deliveryA tumour has antigen X on many of its cells. Scientists make a monoclonal antibody against X and attach a drug. In a trial, 42 of 70 treated patients improve, compared with 21 of 70 receiving the comparison treatment. Explain the advantage of attaching the drug to this antibody.
scheme: 1 · The antibody binds specifically to antigen X.
2 · Attached drug is delivered to antigen-bearing target cells.
3 · This may reduce exposure / damage to healthy cells compared with non-targeted delivery.

questions.prompt: Targeted antibody deliveryA tumour has antigen X on many of its cells. Scientists make a monoclonal antibody against X and attach a drug. In a trial, 42 of 70 treated patients improve, compared with 21 of 70 receiving the comparison treatment. Calculate the difference in improvement percentage points.
scheme: 3 · Difference = 30 percentage points.

questions.prompt: Targeted antibody deliveryA tumour has antigen X on many of its cells. Scientists make a monoclonal antibody against X and attach a drug. In a trial, 42 of 70 treated patients improve, compared with 21 of 70 receiving the comparison treatment. Give one reason the improvement data alone do not establish that the treatment is preferable.
scheme: 1 · Side effects, long-term outcome, cost or comparable trial design must also be evaluated.

questions.prompt: Diagnosing a crop problemA crop has yellow leaves. Some plants also have black spots. An agronomist compares magnesium content, performs a pathogen test and investigates whether spraying a fungicide improves growth. Distinguish two possible causes of yellow leaves and explain a growth effect.
scheme: 1 · Magnesium deficiency can reduce chlorophyll.
2 · A pathogen can damage photosynthetic tissue.
3 · Either can reduce photosynthesis and glucose available for growth.

questions.prompt: Diagnosing a crop problemA crop has yellow leaves. Some plants also have black spots. An agronomist compares magnesium content, performs a pathogen test and investigates whether spraying a fungicide improves growth. Explain why a positive pathogen test does not prove every yellow leaf is caused only by that pathogen.
scheme: 1 · The test identifies presence / a marker, not all causes of every symptom.
2 · Mineral deficiency or other environmental causes may coexist.

questions.prompt: Diagnosing a crop problemA crop has yellow leaves. Some plants also have black spots. An agronomist compares magnesium content, performs a pathogen test and investigates whether spraying a fungicide improves growth. Design a controlled comparison of the fungicide’s effect.
scheme: 1 · Randomly allocate similar affected plants to fungicide and control groups.
2 · Keep nutrient supply, light, water and other conditions constant.
3 · Repeat with enough plants and compare mean growth using the same measurement interval.

questions.prompt: Diagnosing a crop problemA crop has yellow leaves. Some plants also have black spots. An agronomist compares magnesium content, performs a pathogen test and investigates whether spraying a fungicide improves growth. Explain how an intact cuticle and a defensive chemical can help plants.
scheme: 1 · A cuticle reduces pathogen entry as a physical barrier.
2 · A defensive chemical can inhibit microbes or deter herbivores.

questions.prompt: Comparing nervous and hormonal controlConditionReaction time 1 / msReaction time 2 / msReaction time 3 / msQuiet210220230Distraction270280290 Calculate the percentage increase in mean reaction time with distraction.
scheme: 1 · Means 220 ms and 280 ms (1).
3 · 27.3% to 3 significant figures (1).

questions.prompt: Comparing nervous and hormonal controlConditionReaction time 1 / msReaction time 2 / msReaction time 3 / msQuiet210220230Distraction270280290 Explain how an impulse crosses a synapse.
scheme: 1 · Impulse triggers release of a neurotransmitter (1).
2 · Chemical diffuses across gap (1).
3 · Binds to receptors on next neurone and triggers a new electrical impulse (1).

questions.prompt: Comparing nervous and hormonal controlConditionReaction time 1 / msReaction time 2 / msReaction time 3 / msQuiet210220230Distraction270280290 Compare nervous and hormonal coordination.
scheme: 1 · Nervous signals travel along neurones; hormones are carried in blood (1).
2 · Nervous responses generally faster/shorter lasting and more localised; hormonal responses generally slower/longer lasting (1).

questions.prompt: Comparing nervous and hormonal controlConditionReaction time 1 / msReaction time 2 / msReaction time 3 / msQuiet210220230Distraction270280290 Suggest two ways to improve the validity of this comparison.
scheme: 1 · Test same people in both conditions with order randomised (1).
2 · Control sleep/caffeine/practice and other distractions, or use more participants (1).

questions.prompt: Negative feedbackA fasting person has falling blood glucose concentration. For the thyroxine question, use this information: the pituitary releases TSH, which stimulates the thyroid gland to release thyroxine. Explain how glucagon restores blood glucose concentration.
scheme: 1 · Pancreas detects low blood glucose/releases glucagon (1).
2 · Glucagon travels to liver in blood (1).
3 · Stimulates conversion of glycogen to glucose (1).
4 · Glucose released into blood raises concentration (1).

questions.prompt: Negative feedbackA fasting person has falling blood glucose concentration. For the thyroxine question, use this information: the pituitary releases TSH, which stimulates the thyroid gland to release thyroxine. Explain why this is negative feedback.
scheme: 1 · Response opposes the initial fall (1).
2 · As concentration returns to normal, stimulation/glucagon secretion decreases (1).

questions.prompt: Negative feedbackA fasting person has falling blood glucose concentration. For the thyroxine question, use this information: the pituitary releases TSH, which stimulates the thyroid gland to release thyroxine. Explain how adrenaline prepares the body for action.
scheme: 1 · Increases heart rate (1).
2 · Increases delivery of oxygen and glucose to muscles for increased respiration (1).

questions.prompt: Negative feedbackA fasting person has falling blood glucose concentration. For the thyroxine question, use this information: the pituitary releases TSH, which stimulates the thyroid gland to release thyroxine. Explain how thyroxine secretion is controlled when its concentration becomes too high.
scheme: 1 · High thyroxine inhibits pituitary release of TSH (1).
2 · Less TSH stimulates thyroid, reducing thyroxine secretion (1).

questions.prompt: Reproductive hormone interactionsA clinic treats some cases of infertility with hormones. Success is not guaranteed. State the roles of FSH and LH during fertility treatment.
scheme: 1 · FSH stimulates maturation of eggs (1).
2 · LH stimulates ovulation/release of an egg (1).

questions.prompt: Reproductive hormone interactionsA clinic treats some cases of infertility with hormones. Success is not guaranteed. Explain how oestrogen and progesterone help regulate the menstrual cycle.
scheme: 1 · Oestrogen stimulates rebuilding uterus lining (1).
2 · Oestrogen inhibits FSH and stimulates LH release (1).
3 · Progesterone maintains uterus lining (1).
4 · Progesterone inhibits FSH and LH (1).

questions.prompt: Reproductive hormone interactionsA clinic treats some cases of infertility with hormones. Success is not guaranteed. A clinic reports 72 births from 240 treatment cycles. Calculate its birth rate per treatment cycle as a percentage.
Reproductive hormone interactionsA clinic treats some cases of infertility with hormones. Success is not guaranteed. Give one benefit and one risk or disadvantage of IVF.
scheme: 1 · Can enable an infertile couple to have a child (1).
2 · Multiple births/hormone side effects/emotional or financial cost; one valid disadvantage (1).

questions.prompt: Meiosis and inheritanceA recessive allele a causes a genetic condition. A carrier Aa has a child with a person aa who has the condition. Use a genetic cross to find the probability of a child having the condition. Give a decimal probability.
scheme: 1 · Carrier gametes A and a; affected parent gamete a (1).
2 · Offspring Aa and aa in equal proportions (1).
3 · Probability 1/2 or 50% (1).

questions.prompt: Meiosis and inheritanceA recessive allele a causes a genetic condition. A carrier Aa has a child with a person aa who has the condition. Explain how meiosis and fertilisation maintain chromosome number across generations.
scheme: 1 · Meiosis halves chromosome number in gametes (1).
2 · Fertilisation joins/fuses two gamete nuclei (1).
3 · Restores the full chromosome number in the zygote (1).

questions.prompt: Meiosis and inheritanceA recessive allele a causes a genetic condition. A carrier Aa has a child with a person aa who has the condition. Explain why siblings can have different phenotypes even with the same parents.
scheme: 1 · Sexual reproduction produces different combinations of parental alleles (1).
2 · Environmental differences can also affect phenotype (1).

questions.prompt: Meiosis and inheritanceA recessive allele a causes a genetic condition. A carrier Aa has a child with a person aa who has the condition. Evaluate using the result of this cross to predict the outcomes for exactly two children.
scheme: 1 · Probability applies independently to each conception (1).
2 · It does not guarantee that exactly one of two children will have the condition (1).

questions.prompt: Antibiotic resistance and genetic engineeringA hospital finds that an increasing proportion of bacteria are resistant to an antibiotic. Explain how resistance becomes more common and how prescribing decisions can slow this process.
scheme: 1 · Random mutation creates an allele giving resistance/variation already exists.
2 · Antibiotic creates a selection pressure.
3 · Susceptible bacteria are killed.
4 · Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce rapidly.
5 · Resistance allele is passed to offspring, increasing its frequency.
6 · Prescribing antibiotics only when needed reduces selection pressure. Accept completion of the prescribed course as an alternative control, with a correct explanation.
questions.note: Award one mark per distinct valid linked point, maximum 6.

questions.prompt: Antibiotic resistance and genetic engineeringA hospital finds that an increasing proportion of bacteria are resistant to an antibiotic. Describe how bacteria can be genetically engineered to produce human insulin.
scheme: 1 · Human insulin gene is isolated using enzymes (1).
2 · Gene inserted into a vector/plasmid using enzymes (1).
3 · Vector introduces gene into bacteria (1).
4 · Modified bacteria are grown and express the gene to produce insulin, which is collected/purified (1).

questions.prompt: Interdependence and samplingA field has area 800 m². Twenty 0.5 m² quadrats contain a total of 150 clover plants. Fewer clover plants are found near a shaded hedge. Estimate the total number of clover plants in the field.
scheme: 1 · Area sampled = 20 x 0.5 = 10 m² (1).
2 · Density = 150/10 = 15 plants/m² (1).
3 · Estimate = 15 x 800 = 12000 plants (1).

questions.prompt: Interdependence and samplingA field has area 800 m². Twenty 0.5 m² quadrats contain a total of 150 clover plants. Fewer clover plants are found near a shaded hedge. Design an investigation of the effect of distance from the hedge on clover abundance.
scheme: 1 · Place a tape/transect perpendicular to hedge (1).
2 · Sample quadrats at regular measured distances (1).
3 · Count clover using a consistent inclusion rule and record light intensity/other relevant factor (1).
4 · Repeat parallel transects and calculate mean abundance at each distance (1).

questions.prompt: Interdependence and samplingA field has area 800 m². Twenty 0.5 m² quadrats contain a total of 150 clover plants. Fewer clover plants are found near a shaded hedge. Explain why the association with shade does not prove that light is the only cause.
scheme: 1 · Other factors may vary with distance (1).
2 · For example water/mineral availability/trampling/competition (1).
3 · Need control or additional measurement/manipulation of these variables to test causation (1).

questions.prompt: Carbon and water cyclesA restoration project plants 400 trees. In a simplified model, each tree removes an average of 12 kg carbon dioxide per year. In practice, the value varies with tree age and environmental conditions. Calculate the total carbon dioxide removed per year in this model.
scheme: 2 · 4800 kg per year (1).

questions.prompt: Carbon and water cyclesA restoration project plants 400 trees. In a simplified model, each tree removes an average of 12 kg carbon dioxide per year. In practice, the value varies with tree age and environmental conditions. Explain how carbon from dead leaves can return to the atmosphere.
scheme: 1 · Microorganisms/decomposers break down dead material (1).
2 · Their respiration releases carbon dioxide (1).

questions.prompt: Carbon and water cyclesA restoration project plants 400 trees. In a simplified model, each tree removes an average of 12 kg carbon dioxide per year. In practice, the value varies with tree age and environmental conditions. Explain how water is continually recycled between the sea, atmosphere and land.
scheme: 1 · Evaporation from sea/land and transpiration from plants move water into air (1).
2 · Water vapour condenses into clouds and falls as precipitation (1).
3 · Runoff/rivers/groundwater return water to the sea (1).

questions.prompt: Carbon and water cyclesA restoration project plants 400 trees. In a simplified model, each tree removes an average of 12 kg carbon dioxide per year. In practice, the value varies with tree age and environmental conditions. Explain how deforestation can increase atmospheric carbon dioxide.
scheme: 1 · Fewer trees remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis (1).
2 · Burning felled trees releases carbon dioxide (1).
3 · Decay/respiration of dead biomass also releases carbon dioxide (1).

questions.prompt: Keeping warm and conserving waterA runner finishes training in cold dry air. Core temperature falls slightly and blood becomes more concentrated because water has been lost. No water is drunk immediately. Explain how shivering and vasoconstriction oppose the temperature fall.
scheme: 1 · Shivering involves repeated muscle contraction and increased respiration.
2 · Energy is transferred to thermal stores.
3 · Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow near the skin.
4 · This reduces energy transfer to the surroundings.

questions.prompt: Keeping warm and conserving waterA runner finishes training in cold dry air. Core temperature falls slightly and blood becomes more concentrated because water has been lost. No water is drunk immediately. Explain the ADH response to the more concentrated blood.
scheme: 1 · A change in blood water concentration is detected in the brain.
2 · The pituitary releases more ADH.
3 · Kidney tubules become more permeable to water.
4 · More water is reabsorbed into blood, producing a smaller volume of concentrated urine.

questions.prompt: Keeping warm and conserving waterA runner finishes training in cold dry air. Core temperature falls slightly and blood becomes more concentrated because water has been lost. No water is drunk immediately. Explain why this is negative feedback.
scheme: 1 · The responses oppose the original change in water concentration.
2 · As conditions return towards normal, the corrective ADH signal decreases.

questions.prompt: Researching a brain injuryA patient has impaired balance after a brain injury. MRI shows damage near the cerebellum. Researchers consider electrical stimulation during a clinically necessary procedure. State the normal function of the cerebellum and explain one limitation of linking the scan to the symptom.
scheme: 1 · The cerebellum coordinates movement / balance.
2 · Connected pathways may also be affected, so the symptom does not isolate one region’s function.

questions.prompt: Researching a brain injuryA patient has impaired balance after a brain injury. MRI shows damage near the cerebellum. Researchers consider electrical stimulation during a clinically necessary procedure. Evaluate electrical stimulation as evidence for brain function.
scheme: 1 · A reproducible response can link activation of a region to a function.
2 · Complex connections mean stimulation may influence other regions.
3 · Delicate brain tissue creates a risk of irreversible harm.
4 · Informed consent and likely clinical benefit must justify the procedure.

questions.prompt: Researching a brain injuryA patient has impaired balance after a brain injury. MRI shows damage near the cerebellum. Researchers consider electrical stimulation during a clinically necessary procedure. The patient looks from a near object to a distant one. Explain accommodation.
scheme: 1 · Ciliary muscles relax.
2 · Suspensory ligaments tighten.
3 · The lens is pulled thinner.
4 · It refracts light less strongly to focus the distant object on the retina.

questions.prompt: Assessing food-production choicesA farm’s feed contains 6000 kg dry biomass and its livestock gain 480 kg dry biomass. A proposed system reduces animal movement and controls temperature. The farm also considers replacing part of its output with fungal mycoprotein. Calculate biomass transfer efficiency.
scheme: 1 · Efficiency = gain / input × 100.

questions.prompt: Assessing food-production choicesA farm’s feed contains 6000 kg dry biomass and its livestock gain 480 kg dry biomass. A proposed system reduces animal movement and controls temperature. The farm also considers replacing part of its output with fungal mycoprotein. Explain two reasons the remaining input biomass does not become new livestock biomass.
scheme: 1 · Some food is not digested and is egested.
2 · Some absorbed material is lost through respiration / excretion, such as carbon dioxide, water or urea.

questions.prompt: Assessing food-production choicesA farm’s feed contains 6000 kg dry biomass and its livestock gain 480 kg dry biomass. A proposed system reduces animal movement and controls temperature. The farm also considers replacing part of its output with fungal mycoprotein. Explain how the proposed livestock system could increase yield and give one drawback.
scheme: 1 · Less movement reduces energy transferred in muscle activity.
2 · Controlled temperature reduces energy demand for keeping warm.
3 · A valid drawback concerns welfare, disease, cost or resource use.

questions.prompt: Assessing food-production choicesA farm’s feed contains 6000 kg dry biomass and its livestock gain 480 kg dry biomass. A proposed system reduces animal movement and controls temperature. The farm also considers replacing part of its output with fungal mycoprotein. Explain one requirement for producing fungal mycoprotein and evaluate a potential benefit and limitation.
scheme: 1 · A suitable carbohydrate supply, oxygen for aerobic growth or controlled temperature supports fungal growth in fermenters.
2 · A valid benefit includes protein production with potentially less livestock demand.
3 · A limitation such as energy / input costs, environmental impacts or consumer acceptance must be considered.
